In the quiet morning, before the world has fully turned its face toward the sun, I find myself awake, aware of the soft hum of electricity and the occasional bird testing its voice. There is a kind of spaciousness here in this hour, a blank page of a day asking to be written. A hundred thoughts drift across the surface of my mind, some familiar, some new, and I am tempted to chase each one like a child chasing soap bubbles across a lawn. What to capture? What to let go? The invitation of “write whatever comes to you” feels at once liberating and daunting, as if the limitless possible narratives could swamp the little vessel of my attention. Yet there is always a beginning, a single word placed after another, a small bridge extending over the unknown. This bridge is what we call language. Through it we cross into the landscapes of the possible.

I think of the first time I read a novel under the covers with a flashlight, convinced that I was smuggling treasure in the dark. The book was old, its pages yellowed, smelling faintly of dust and ink, but between those covers entire worlds unfolded. A pirate ship creaked in a storm. A lonely island stretched under an endless sky. A boy not much older than I faced choices that seemed enormous. Under my blanket, I felt the thrill of accompanying him, of being let in on secrets too big for daylight. Perhaps that was one of the moments when I understood that words are doors, not merely sounds.

So what doors do I open now? The world outside my window is quieter than the one on the page, but its quiet is full of layers. The leaves stir with a breeze I cannot see. Far away, a train sounds its horn, punctuating the stillness with a long note that fades into memory. The neighbor’s dog barks, then settles. Somewhere, someone is making coffee, and the aroma will soon drift in through the open window. I am here, a collection of sensations and thoughts, bound together by a curious desire to translate this moment into words.

Perhaps I write because doing so is a way of paying attention. To write is to slow down, to notice the texture of experience. When I describe the way sunlight filters through the leaves, I am also standing in that light. When I choose a verb, I am considering movement, choosing pace. Writing is not simply about recording events; it is about creating a relationship between perception and expression. And in that space, something alchemical happens. The mundane is transformed into the meaningful. The unnoticed becomes illuminated. Even sorrow, when given shape by a sentence, reveals its hidden textures, its passages of tenderness.

There were seasons when I could not find words, when the pages stayed blank. Grief can be like that, a storm that flattens every structure you built to shelter your voice. In those times, silence felt heavy, but even then, there was an undercurrent of meaning. The way a friend set down a cup of tea beside me without a word. The day the sky cleared after days of rain, and the light hit the puddles so that each seemed to hold a small world. Eventually, the urge to speak returned, tentative at first, then in a rush, and the pen moved again, finding its way across the page. Writing became not a luxury, but a necessity, a way of making sense of what felt senseless.

I smile thinking of the absurdity of language, too. How else can we speak of what we do not fully understand except through metaphor? We say time flies, as if it had wings. We call someone a rock, as if they are stone. We build cathedrals of idea and feeling out of breath and ink. The same word can be a balm or a blade. This playfulness, this capacity for shifting meaning, delights me. It is the dancing ground where poets and comedians and lovers meet. It is the terrain of possibility.

As the morning ripens into day, the constraints of time make themselves felt. Words must gather pace, not because there is nothing left to say, but because there is too much, and any attempt to say everything would be like trying to capture a river in a jar. Even within the frame of a thousand words, there are choices. Do I tell you about the time I stood on a cliff and watched whales breach, their massive bodies arching through air as spray caught the light like jewels? Or about an elderly neighbor who plants sunflowers each year because his wife loved them, and though she is gone, the sunflowers keep returning? Do I speak of how technology both connects and isolates us, of how a screen can be a window and a wall? Or do I simply let you sit here with me in the morning light, sharing this pause?

Perhaps that is enough. To sit, to attend, to let the mind wander and return. Outside, the day calls, carrying with it tasks and joys. I will answer, stepping into its current. But for now, there is this space, these words, this line extending from me to you. If you are reading, then in some small way, we are sitting together, two points connected across distance by the fragile, resilient thread of language. In that connection there is comfort, a reminder that we are not alone in our wondering. The words end, but the listening can continue.

So here is a thought as the kettle begins to boil: each moment is a point and a line, a dot on the map and a path outward. We cannot see all destinations, but we can choose how to travel, with curiosity, care, willingness to be surprised. The sun is higher now, the birds insistent, the day unfolding whether I write or not, but for this moment I have written.
